utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I note the absence of Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Sainovic this morning. Mr. O'Sullivan, before the proceedings started yesterday there was a waiver from Mr. Milutinovic for his absence. I understand one will be produced for today. Thank you. And, Mr. Fila, do I take it that Mr. Sainovic is content that the proceedings continue in his absence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything's fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning again, Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Cross-examination will continue from Mr. Hannis probably for the next session till the break, and then there will be re-examination by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us on Tuesday I think it was about after this global plan or the plan for combatting terrorism came out in July of 1998 that around the 22nd or 23rd of July there was a meeting in Pristina and at page 22197, you told us that officers of the Army of Yugoslavia and police chiefs of the secretariats and maybe commanders lower-level were present at the meeting to discuss how that was going to be carried out. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was that meeting held?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the offices of the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you personally attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was your role at the meeting? Did you speak or participate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who led the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to this preparatory meeting for the activities to be carried out with the officers of the VJ were present, I think it was Generals Lazarevic and Pavkovic who spoke and who explained either something regarding the plan or something of the sort; and then they gave guide-lines for implementation of that plan, what activities had to be carried out in the future, and that in relation to that first action that was to be carried out documents were distributed to officers who were to participate in that action and that's how it concluded. That was the preparation for that first action and for future activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did General Lukic attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he speak to the group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I wouldn't be able to claim anything with certainty. It was quite a long time ago, so I don't remember who spoke, what they said. I don't remember the details, but you can probably find it in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you seen minutes of that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen a lot of minutes, a lot of documents. To tell you the truth, there is quite a lot of facts in them and it's difficult for me to remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is happening at more or less the same time as the meeting in 6D798?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if it's the same day or shortly thereafter. General or then-Colonel Delic testified, Your Honour, and at page 19501 and 19574 he made mention of a meeting which I believe is the same meeting based on the description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You remember, Mr. Mijatovic, looking yesterday at the incomplete minute in which there's reference to something called the global plan. We also looked at it earlier in the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the meeting that you're now talking about is around the same time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether that was that specific meeting or a day before, a day later, whether there was another meeting in relation to that action, to tell you the truth I'm not sure any longer. But I know quite certainly that preparations were made with officers for that first action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in discussing this on the 12th of February during your testimony you mentioned that the MUP staff didn't exert any influence nor could it affect course of anti-terrorist activities because the units acted on the basis of a plan that had been prepared for a particular action and officers who were in charge of those units were responsible for implementation of the plan. Activities were carried out in the field. The units were controlled by radio equipment that the MUP staff could not monitor because we used different frequencies. I want to ask you a question about that and I'd like to show you Exhibit P1434, and I can hand you a hard copy with help from the usher. Just to have a quick look at the first page so you can see this is an order from the Pristina Corps command dated the 19th of September, 1998, to support MUP forces in breaking up Siptar terrorists in the general Cicavica sector. By the way, did you ever see that document before today?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw it during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what I'd like you to look at is item number 8 which I think is at page 8 in the B/C/S, near the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the English, Your Honours, it's at page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's the section on command and communications, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I, if I may, for a second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can't see this document on the list, so if my colleague could help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I usually don't put it on my binder unless it's on a list, but maybe I missed it. I'll have my case manager check and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, it's checked, it's on our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, do you see that, item number 8, and in the second paragraph it says: "Arrange communications according to the communications plan to be drawn up by the chief of communications Pristina Corps and the MUP"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know who in the MUP would be responsible for helping draw up a communications plan for this kind of joint action?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, a chief of communications in the Pristina SUP was involved in this because these technical matters concerning the staff and communications was done by him -- were done by him. And in the staff we also had Milan Cankovic, who was also dealing with signals and communications. When I spoke about that, I was not referring to the plan, I was referring to the technical capabilities, because the units out on the field were using different frequencies and the staff was not able to follow the course of, say, an action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about Mr. Deretic from the staff, did he have any involvement in communications?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no Djuretic in the staff, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I may have mispronounced, Deretic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was precisely Deretic who was chief of communications section in the secretariat, and as far as I know, he was in charge of communications in the entire region of Kosovo and Metohija and he provided support to other secretariats as well in addition to doing his job in Pristina. And I think he is going to come here as a witness and perhaps he would be better-placed to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And now if we could look at Exhibit P1993 also connected to this issue of communication. I'll trade you documents with the help of the usher. We've looked at this one before, Colonel. This one is from the meeting held in the MUP staff on the 11th of May, and I want to look at page 12 in the English, Your Honours, and for you, Colonel, I think it's page 5 of the B/C/S and it's under item 12 where Commander Colic is speaking, and I think it's the fifth bullet point under him. He says: "I gave three USW radio stations to VJ commander Jelic [Realtime transcript read in error "Delic"] to use a month ago and as this is PJP equipment I requested them back but they have not returned the radio stations to date." Was the MUP sharing some of their radios with the VJ so that they could communicate with each other or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said earlier, I did not go out in the field. I don't know what they did out in the field, but quite definitely they had cooperation between them and they coordinated their activities. And in order for them to be able to do that, they had to have appropriate radio stations. I guess it was done on purpose in this way so that commanders from the police and the army could communicate between themselves during those actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On page 6, line 23 I think the reference should be to Jelic rather than Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel. And in further discussion about those early joint actions, a question came up to my mind about what happened in the field if there were a disagreement between the VJ commander and the MUP commander on the ground about how the action should be carried out. Who resolved that? Was there a higher authority or did each one go up their own chain and those two higher commanders got together? Do you know how that worked?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, there were no particular problems between the units participating in anti-terrorist activities and actions. There were no problems and there was no need for anything to be resolved. Somehow they always managed to understand each other and resolve any problems, if there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge that was true throughout the war during these joint actions, right? Even though there wasn't formal subordination ever accomplished, the coordination on the ground between the VJ and the MUP worked pretty well, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to show you Exhibit P1693. I'll hand you a hard copy of this one as well. Colonel, this is a summary or a survey of events and information bearing on the security situation for the 30th of April and the 1st of May, 1999. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see some. Now, whether I saw this particular one, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is a-- it appears to be a daily report that comes from the MUP staff to the Ministry of the Interior, right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report produced by the staff on the basis of daily reports of the secretariats of the interior in Kosovo and Metohija which was then forwarded to the Ministry of the Interior to certain people, and you can see to whom it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us that because the NATO bombing you had some problems about being in communication with your units out in the field. But how did you get the information that went in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yes, there were difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the information in this particular report seems to include information from out in the field, how were you obtaining that information to put in these reports?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such situations, we were forced to solve this via couriers, which is to say that a courier from the secretariat would come to Pristina bringing these daily reports; and we used the same principle as in the previous period. We would put it all together and send it to the ministry. Sometimes it would happen, depending on the situation on the ground, depending on activities and where they were carried out, that some reports were late. There was a two or three-day delay in these reports arriving and then once they would arrive we would put it in our report even though it wasn't exactly timely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you would look at I think it's the last page item number 4 has information about persons who fled the territory of Kosovo. Do you recall, was that information that was generally placed in these reports?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we had such information, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see in the third paragraph under that item it says: "Between 24 April and 30 April a total of 715.158 persons belonging to the Siptar national minority left the territory." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't know if you'll recall, I think yesterday we looked at Exhibit P2166, wherein it contained information about the actions that had been carried out pursuant to the plan between the 22nd of July and the end of September 1998, and it made reference to the total -- to the percentage of the total population in Kosovo that had been involved in connection with that. And you may recall, I don't have the exact number, but the total population was about 1.500.000. Would you agree with me, this number's about half the total population of Kosovo leaving in one week in April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it looks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, if this is the position of the Prosecution, then we would like to know it because their expert witness showed us completely different numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is you -- oh, I'm sorry, no, it is a Prosecution exhibit, which has been available throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I have another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to try to understand what Mr. Lukic's point is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because the Prosecution at that time claimed that there were 2.200.000 people in Kosovo; now we see the number of 15 and claiming that half of the population left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. This, though, is a document of the MUP and when you're building a case as a Prosecutor, you're free to rely on any material you have which taken together might establish a point that you seek to make. How to interpret this in the overall context of all the material bearing on the numbers leaving Kosovo or on the total population of Kosovo is a matter for us at the end of the day once parties have addressed us. But at the moment leading evidence of this nature seems entirely appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And just to be precise, Colonel, I will indicate that the number mentioned at that inter-departmental staff meeting on the 29th of October was 1.561.585 residents as being the total residents in Kosovo and Metohija according to, I think, it was General Pavkovic speaking at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just going back to the transcript, line 21 there of page 10 it's at the end of the day after parties have addressed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I have another question about this document. When we were looking at some other document on the 12th of February, you at page 22218 explained that every internal organizational unit of the ministry had its own initial number for the documents that it sent out, and you went on to say, since the staff in Pristina, the MUP staff, didn't have its own number, this registration number it was assigned this number and that's why the A was added in order to make a distinction. But in this report from the MUP staff to the Ministry of the Interior, if you can look at the first page, you'll see the number is 10-121/2, there's no A attached here. Doesn't that mean that the MUP staff is an organizational unit and it has its own numbering system?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see number 10-121/2, the 1st of May, 1999. I can't really tell you where this number comes from, but I know for a fact that the MUP staff was never an organizational unit either before or in 1999, nor was it able to have its own number because according to the regulations as far as I know only an official organizational unit could have been issued with a number according to the rule book of the ministry. Where this number comes from, I don't know, I don't know whether something has been changed within the ministry and then, for example, the police administration had numbers beginning with 10. I don't see the prefix here, so I wouldn't be able to comment, but I know for a fact that the staff was not an organizational unit of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can I take you back to the first line of page 11 where you say: "Just to be precise, Colonel, I mention that that number mentioned was 1 and a half million residents," was that a reference to something said at the inter-departmental staff meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's in P2166.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, help me with this. I know you've said that several times that the MUP staff was not an organizational unit, but can you explain to me, where do we find the definition of organizational units? Can you give me a precise reference to a document or a rule?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I speak on the basis of my recollections. I'm not a lawyer, I didn't draft these documents, and I'm sure that there are other people, the experts, who would be able to tell you more, who would be interpreting regulations and so on. Whether this was some rule book on organization or some other things, I really don't know. But I know for a fact that the staff was not an organizational unit of the ministry and it was not something like administrations within the ministry or the organizational units which had certain territory within Serbia that they cover, such as secretariats and so on. But I know certainly that the staff was not an organizational unit. It was a provisional ad hoc body that was established by way of decisions and existed for a year or so. We saw some of the decisions. Had it been a permanent organizational unit, there would have been no need to issue a decision establishing the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me follow-up on that. You at page 22216, line 15, said: "The staff does not belong to that group that I mentioned a while ago, it's not an organizational unit. The staff was a temporary, an auxiliary, body of the ministry." But didn't you tell us that the staff had first been created in approximately 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I said it was established in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1990, that's when the first staff was established, after the break-up of the SFRY started and when the other republics withdrew their forces, then Serbia, the Republic of Serbia, took over this obligation and established this first staff. I don't know exactly what its name was, but I know that it does date back to then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So how many years does it take before it changes from a temporary body to a permanent one?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This temporary body was never transformed into a permanent one in terms of being an organizational unit of the ministry. That never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You -- I think you've told us before, you're not a lawyer and you would agree you're not an expert on the law on state administration or the rules, right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But this non-organizational unit of the MUP was given task in connection with organizational units like the SAJ and the JSO, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand your question. In what sense do you mean this? What kind of tasks in connection with the SAJ and the rest? Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in the exhibit that created -- the decision that created the staff in June of 1998, we saw the task of the MUP staff, and although you told us that apparently none of those were implemented, although you and I have a disagreement about that, those envisioned tasks that the MUP staff would have in connection with non -- with organizational units. So I guess my question is: The non-organizational unit, the MUP staff, had some authority over the organizational units, right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it was resolved or envisaged, but it doesn't mean that the staff is an organizational unit. Of course as for the implementation of these tasks, that never happened within the staff and we've already said why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we next look at Exhibit 1D680. I can hand you a copy of that and trade you, Colonel. This is a document from the minister of the interior, Mr. Stojiljkovic. It's dated the 11th of May, 1999. The first page listed as a draft decree on promotion of General Lukic, and if you could turn to the second page, the second text of that document, it's the minister writing to President Milutinovic in the first paragraph he says: "I hereby propose you issue a decree promoting Sreten Lukic to the rank of lieutenant-general." But I'm interested in the last paragraph where the minister says: "In the past year Lukic had excelled in successful command and control of the MUP units engaged in the prevention of terrorism in Kosovo." Now, can you explain to me how you fit that in with your view that the MUP staff didn't have any ability and actually didn't exercise any kind of control over the units engaged in preventing terrorism in Kosovo? Was the minister misinformed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained, or rather, I have given evidence as to what happened and how on the ground. One thing was written in the decision, that is a fact, but things happened differently. It is correct that the minister of the interior proposes this promotion, and that is also done in case of decorations. And actually, in these proposals, there is always some kind of an explanation. The minister of course signs that document, which is then sent to the person who makes the actual decision, but the minister certainly doesn't write that document himself. One of his co-workers does that, or rather, one of his clerks, if I can put it that way, or someone who prepares documents for him. I don't know who it was that did that and whether that person knows at all this individual, rather, whether this individual knows what was done and how in Kosovo and Metohija. In the decision on the establishment of the staff there is that item number 2, as it stands, and it is possible that the author of this explanation, on the basis of this, provided that explanation because there has to be some explanation in order to have a proposal accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that this explanation was made up and it's not true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that the author of this text intentionally invented that. I'm assuming that the man didn't know what the situation was really like in Kosovo and Metohija and when looking at this decision, that is the explanation that he provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I suggest, Colonel, an alternative explanation may be that the minister and whoever authored this actually did know and they were correct because General Lukic was attending Joint Command meetings through 1998 and 1999, as he's told us in his own interview with the OTP; and you didn't know about that because you didn't know even about the existence of Joint Command. So isn't that a possible alternative explanation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I was aware of this term but that I never learned -- and actually I'm still convinced that this Joint Command did not exist because I did not perceive in any way its existence. I did not hear of any tasks coming from it, I didn't feel its existence quite simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So now are you saying that General Lukic is mistaken or not telling the truth when he told OTP in his interview that there was a Joint Command and he went to the meetings in 1998 and 1999? Is that what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know. I said that I briefly looked at this statement and I saw this place where he says the so-called Joint Command, which means -- well, if he says "so-called," it was my understanding that it was some kind of a self-styled body. But if he stated in that statement that a Joint Command did exist, I don't know about those motives, but I know how I felt this and whether I felt the existence of this command at all. He never mentioned that he was going to Joint Command meetings or that he come with tasks or assignments from the Joint Command or did he order us to make some kind of reports for the Joint Command or to inform this Joint Command about how it was that we acted in accordance with some order coming from that Joint Command, "naredjenje," I mean, really, I do not remember any such case. I don't know how it could have existed without myself and other members of the staff being aware of its existence. I simply cannot explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I waited for the answer to finish because I believe that is courteous, Your Honour. You said that documents should not be shown while the Prosecutor is quoting, but when the Prosecutor is misquoting then the documents should be shown. Yesterday I kept silent, although I did want to get up. You cannot consider it to be a quotation if not everything is said, but Mr. Lukic's interview says the so-called Joint Command. So please, could the witness be shown exactly where it is that the Prosecutor found General Lukic admitting to the existence of a Joint Command, as the Prosecutor had phrased his question, and let me see that too. Because I -- as Aristotle says, I am fond of Plato, but I'm even more fond of the truth. I really appreciate and have high regard for Mr. Hannis, but even more for the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us your best quote on this, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he does refer to it as the so-called Joint Command at page 48 of his interview, but he answers other questions and he calls it "Joint Command." And I gave -- I listed to all those page numbers yesterday. I don't have the list to hand at the moment. Pages 84 to 85, 97 to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It starts at 48 to 50 I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we have the list, but is there an example you could perhaps put up that the witness can see of a clear statement of the term Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At page 98 -- well, let's start on 97 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need the exhibit number first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's Exhibit Number 948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're talking about 97 in the English, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 97 -- it's one document now, it's merged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, of course. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm starting with a question from Kevin Curtis, OTP investigator. And they've been talking about the meeting in July 1998 with Mr. Milosevic where the plan that we've been talking about came up. And if I may, Your Honour, I'll start from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis says: "That conversation when you brought up about the meeting in Belgrade was prompted by me asking you Sainovic's role in the Joint Command in Kosovo. Was the Joint Command discussed at that meeting in Belgrade at the end of June, beginning of July, let me put it a different way. Was the Joint Command encompassed in part of the plan that was presented by General Pavkovic?" And there's the B/C/S translation of the question, and Mr. Lukic's answer, which in English is page 98. "It's not known to me who took part in composing this plan but Mr. Minic, Sainovic, Matkovic, and Andjelkovic were present at this meeting that I already mentioned." Your Honour, I don't want to read the rest unless you tell me I need to. But Mr. Lukic says at the top of page 99: "As far as I remember the details, it was said that Mr. Minic, Sainovic, Matkovic, and Andjelkovic would be in Kosovo, but wasn't specified that there would be special structure which would implement the plan." Kevin Curtis then asks: "How did the formation of the Joint Command come about?" And then Mr. Lukic said: "In effect, the composition that I have mentioned was the command, the Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, it doesn't say "Joint Command." It says "zdruzenu komandu," which is a different term so he's not clear about the term and it's "fakticku."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're challenging this translation, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It wasn't the translation I think, it's taped, so it's the word -- those are words of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but you're challenging the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the translation into English is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can understand why Mr. -- following what's in English here, you can understand the questions that have been put and there's nothing wrong with the questions based on the translation. The issue seems to be one of the translation, which will need to be investigated. What do you say would be the translation of that expression?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whatever translation is, it's -- the words used are different from "zajednicka komanda," which is allegedly the term used for this command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you don't have a translation for this that could help us at the moment? I don't fault you for that, I just want to know if you can assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no I don't. The meaning is the same, the word is different, and I think it's also substantial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But of course at the end of the day it's meaning that matters, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic never made mistake when he mentioned MUP staff because it was a body in which he was, but he obviously made mistake naming this body or if it -- if there is any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask the interpreter whether there is another ready translation of this expression.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Both can be translated as "joint," but indeed it is two different words so it would have to be a synonym in English for joint, whether we could resort to combined again but I guess not because combined has already been used for "objedinjena komanda," so it's different synonyms, different words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, we shall ask CLSS to reflect on this and see if further assistance can be given to the Chamber that all parties will have access to. Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor said in his question that Mr. Lukic admitted to the existence of a Joint Command. I see what Curtis is trying to do here. He tried that with Sainovic, and that is to say to put his own words into somebody else's mouth. Find me a quotation where General Lukic says there is a Joint Command, and I attended its meetings, and in 1990 at that, because this is 1998. We haven't been accused, at least not yet, for 1998, although in this court we're using 80 per cent of our time for 1998. So you said Joint Command and that Lukic admitted that. I don't see 1999 and I don't see any admission. I don't see that in the statement, so I'm not satisfied with what the Prosecutor has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The best way for us to deal with this is to reserve the question of determining this particular objection because there is no rapid way of resolving an issue over the nuances of interpretation of language where a number of words mean joint or combined or unified, and no doubt there are other synonyms that may express a similar but perhaps slightly different idea. So in the rough and tumble of this trial today we can't resolve it. We will reserve that question until we see the final position, including further thoughts of CLSS on how this ought to be translated and comments of the parties on that. Standing the translation that we do have, Mr. Hannis, we see nothing wrong with the approach you took and the question you asked, and we're not persuaded by Mr. Fila's argument that just because Mr. -- or the investigator -- who was the investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Kevin Curtis, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just because he puts words into the witness's mouth, that disables you from asking a question. It's all a question of weight at the end of the day, there will be very substantial arguments to be made by the Defence that because he put words in his mouth, we should give little weight to the response. But that's a matter for assessment in the context of all the evidence bearing on the point. Mr. Fila, I appreciate -- we all appreciate your anxiety where something appears to you to be misleading, but at the end of the day, rest assured, we'll be looking at everything together to see if, in fact, it amounts to the establishment of an active Joint Command and that's very much a live issue for us that has to be viewed in the context of everything we hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is just this last point. I accept that and of course I indeed trust you that you will look into this, but my concern is something different that they insist on something all the time, like those notes and minutes and whatever else. I was just asking the Prosecutor to read out portions that have to do with 1998 or perhaps he should have the indictment include 1998 then rather than 1999 only. Just analyse things, and you will see that we're only dealing with 1998 and that is another part of the story. Let him give me a quotation on 1999. Maybe he will -- well, maybe it's an oversight on my part. 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Fila, there may be other evidence that leads us to the conclusion that what was going on in 1998 was also happening in 1999, although not specifically mentioned in such detail as in 1998. It again is a matter of the appropriate inferences to be drawn from all the evidence. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for taking more time, but I just -- while we have this on the screen the next paragraph, the translation one of the lines starts with: "Yes" and there is no yes in Serbian version. So I think this translation has to be revised anyways completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are things, though, we would expect you to draw our attention to. If you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have time to go through every and each document and check translations; trust me, we don't have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we are sympathetic to the point that's made that there is a limit to human resource in dealing with the material in this case. What we don't accept for one minute is that you have not had time to minutely analyse the interview record of your own client which extends to only 200 and odd pages unlike others in this case. This must be a crucial document that it's inconceivable for you not to have looked at carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope that you're not objecting that we are not working diligently on this case, Your Honour. I think that you cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you telling me, Mr. Lukic, that you have not analysed this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not translation, I didn't find time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find that incomprehensible, Mr. Lukic, incomprehensible. Let's proceed, Mr. Hannis. Have you have a better example that you can put that may not give rise to this controversy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one point, Your Honour, we got the translation a few days ago and at the moment when our case started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why did -- has this just been made available, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is correct. This was the same situation as General Lazarevic. The translation, only the English had been put into the transcript. The video -- the videotape of the interview was provided to the Defence before the trial started. That exhibit was admitted on the 10th of October, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're saying that the English translation has always been available?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, all that can have been supplemented is a B/C/S transcript, surely. You must always have had the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've just told me the English became available --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, the combined transcript became available. How could we compare something that's not combined?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've had the videotape. I'm surprised that you have not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But still my objection to this translation stands, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, and we will treat it as an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if you have other objections to the translation of documents of the significance of this, then these have to be notified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what was the order we made about the provision of a combined transcript in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that you made an order regarding this, but because it came up with General Lazarevic's interview we decided that we should do it for General Lukic too because he's been noticed as a witness who may testify, and anticipating using that transcript with him we thought we should follow the same procedure that was done with General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, these cases, as you know, are conducted in English. I understand there can be many criticisms of that aspect of international criminal procedure, but that's the reality of the situation, and it's the English that counts in the end of the day. And in a document as crucial as this, it's vital that if there are challenges to the English that they are intimated. And the English version has been available for a very long time. However, let's proceed with the evidence. Mr. Hannis, can you find us a clearer example that will not give rise to controversy?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On page 49 we have in the answer of Mr. Lukic to a question about the Joint Command he says: "The people who were there were federal deputy Minister Nikola Sainovic and chairman of the -- chairman of citizens Mr. Minic; there was also Djoko Matkovic, who was either deputy prime minister of the Serbian government or just minister; Zoran Andjelkovic," and if I can skip a couple of lines: "But I must say that these people mentioned before would sometimes meet with military and ministry members and officials with the commander of the Pristina Corps, et cetera, and they would have joint meetings which is why it was referred to sometimes as the Joint Command." And the Serbian term there is "zajednicka komanda."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now do we have an objection to that translation? None is taken. So there is an example, Mr. Mijatovic, of what Mr. Hannis is putting to you. Do you want to comment on that or have you commented as far as you think you can?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, I do have an objection, Your Honour, to this translation as well. Sorry, I had to -- I didn't have time at that moment to compare. First of all, it's obvious that there was a pause which was not recorded in English and when we have this smooth reference like referred, but in Serbian it's not "referred," it's more likely that something is -- I beg the translators to translate "poistovecivanje."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Something that is identified with something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly, not referred, but identified, so something identified with something else, not as is in English, referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, you're able to read the Serbian version of this. Just look at the end of the passage which is highlighted, the darker passage. Do you want to comment any further on the issue of the Joint Command in light of the comments that you're seeing made by Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think I have said enough about what I know about the Joint Command. I really don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, someone is going to have to look at this closely and it has to be done soon because similar questions may yet arise as we go along and it would be helpful to us if we had a clear idea of the areas in which you think the translation requires revisal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This translation, I don't know if it's made by the Prosecutor's office or by CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think the one before was done by the Prosecutor's office and this one also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's obviously the Prosecutor's translation, Your Honour. There are -- there are wishes in this text, not the reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Lukic, I'm not prepared to allow you to say that openly in court. I think you should withdraw that remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I withdraw this remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The situation will be considered by us a little further, and if we have to take steps, we'll take them; if we require you or Mr. Hannis to take steps, then we'll tell you what these are. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you read the whole translation into English and the Serbian version, does the Prosecutor consider this to be General Lukic's admission that there was, in fact, a Joint Command? That's my question. Because one cannot draw that conclusion from this text, whatever language you read it in. It's about 1998, Your Honour. In 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is for later and it's not for Mr. Hannis to answer any questions. Let's get on with the evidence. Move along, please, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before we leave this I want to address one issue raised by Mr. Fila. If we could look at page 111, in the middle of the page Mr. Curtis asked a question and he said: "One thing I didn't ask you is, this Joint Command, where were the meetings held?" Mr. Lukic's answer is translated in English as: "At different places, because the joint commander did not have a building location of its own particular. The meetings, especially at the very beginning, were most often held at the Pristina Corps command. Later on, they were mostly held at the premises of the transitional Executive Council." Colonel, were you aware that General Lukic was attending meetings at the Pristina Corps command and at the temporary or provisional Executive Council office?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even with the most meager knowledge of English, I don't know if there's anyone who speaks English worse than I do, you can see nowhere does it say "zajednicka komandant," joint commander, I can see that, and you know how poor my English is. Where did he get this joint commander from, I have no idea. So this is why documents have to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object to this translation at this point as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I read that as a misprint for Joint Command, I must say. Is that a mistake --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now that I see the B/C/S I think it is Joint Command and not commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But again, it is not "zajednicka" but "zdruzena" there is no word "zajednicka."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're back to the same word as we had a moment ago, which may be command or -- combined or unified or whatever. We understand that, so let's -- and this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let Mr. Hannis find another translation which would be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For the moment, proceed on the basis of what's here, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on page 112, if we could, my last couple of questions from this document for this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it appears to us to be pretty pointless to continue with the cross-examination. The witness has made it abundantly clear that he's not going to accept that there was an organization known as the Joint Command that did anything. So is there any point in any more questions other than to do a bit of grand-standing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's no jury here, and we're getting into a very confused situation because of translation difficulties, and we're really not making any progress in the time that we're spending on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. A point was raised by Mr. Fila in his intervention about nothing in this says that General Lukic went to meetings in 1999. That's the last point I'm trying to address on page 112 about when meetings occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minor point, I didn't say that Lukic said that he didn't go. I said that you did not show that. Now you're showing it and that's okay and I have no objection. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would ask that we go back and look at the record because I think he said it does not appear anywhere in this document that Mr. Lukic went to meetings in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that may be right, Mr. Fila, but let's proceed then and deal with that issue, Mr. Hannis, and then let's move on to other material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, page 112, and now this is Philip Coo asking a question. "So during the time of the bombing where would the Joint Command be most often?" General Lukic answered: "Due to the specific situation in this period, the changes in the locations of the army command as well as the MUP staff or headquarters, the meetings were held at whichever location we could." And then he went on to say: "I'm sorry to interrupt, but now it's all coming back to me, speaking of the places where the meetings were held. They were usually held in basements, but most often they were held in the shelter of Grand Hotel." Now, does that help you remember that General Lukic was also attending meetings in the basement of the Grand Hotel during the bombing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say anything about the time when the air-strikes were ongoing. The situation was chaotic and who met whom where I really can't say. I can't go into details because I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, yesterday or I guess on Wednesday, you were shown a document Exhibit P1996 which are the minutes of the 7 May 1999 meeting where General Dragan Ilic was present and addressed the meeting. Do you remember that meeting? I can get the document for you if you need to, but right now my question is: Do you remember him coming and speaking at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've seen those minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you are listed as attending that meeting. Do you remember being present?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but could we please zoom in a little bit because it's difficult to read. I think it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can hand you a hard copy that will make it easier to go through. It's several pages. And if you want to go through to page 8 of the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we're beginning at the bottom of page 9 and going on to page 10 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- where it talks about the remarks of Dragan Ilic, he mentions a meeting that was held on the 5th of May at the staff of the ministry in Pristina with the chiefs of the SUP and the SUP crime investigation department -- or no, with the crime investigation department. Did you know about that meeting? Did you attend it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And wasn't one of the purposes of that meeting and this meeting here because Ilic, General Ilic, had concerns about what was being done and not being done regarding the investigation of crimes, right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the whole contents. I've read parts of the minutes, but there's an abundance of facts here, I can't remember each and every one, but I did say --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you then to look at bullet point number 4 under Ilic. He talks about: "A meeting was held with VJ top officials at which it was agreed that measures were being applied but they are not sufficient at the moment." That sounds like there were shortcomings in connection with this issue of investigating crimes. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't comment on this because at that meeting he's referring to -- well, I wasn't there and I really don't know what they said there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that he had a meeting with representatives of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you would continue on down to where we see General Lukic contributing to the discussion, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we're on the bottom half of page 10 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you find that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's near the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'm not sure if you find it on that page or the next page, but the second bullet point under General Lukic says: "The number of 27 crimes of murder is not realistic as we have information that a greater number of on-site investigations has been conducted and that the number of criminal reports for this crime is greater." Do you know what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say here it's about crimes. It says it's about 27 crimes of murder and that there is information that more on-site investigations had been carried out and that there were more criminal reports about these crimes. I don't know if this refers to one particular secretariat or is it the overall figure, but certainly the figure transpired from the discussions, and that's why General Lukic drew attention to the fact that when one compares the data this piece of information is incorrect because --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from the reports it was evident that there had been more murders committed --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you can't add anything to what is written down there, then please just tell me that and I will move on. If you will go to General Stevanovic who speaks next, I don't know if that's on that page or that may go over to the following page. Do you see where he's speaking?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And he says: "I want you to concentrate on four assignments in the forthcoming period. " And number 2: "Anti-terrorist actions," the last sentence under that says: "The plan must be approved by the staff and will be carried out together with manoeuvre detachments." Isn't it correct that each SUP was supposed to work on a plan and those plans were to be approved by the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I can't find this. Can you help me locate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It should be under General Stevanovic speaking and the second point.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you see the last sentence under that item, it says: "The plan must be approved by the staff," right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just see what plan this is about. Excuse me. Yes, General Stevanovic said that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I know he said that, I can read that, but is it true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now. I don't remember having seen any plan drawn up by the secretariat and submitted for approval. I'm not saying that there was no such plan, but it's quite normal for a plan to be looked at to see that there are no omissions, no faults in it, but the secretariats planned those things on their own, organized them and implemented them. In view of the fact that it was General Stevanovic saying this, I assume -- well, I don't know how precisely the person taking the minutes formulated this, but General Stevanovic don't have another address to which such plans could be sent, so I really don't know whether it was he or General Lukic who approved those plans. As I said, I never saw any such plan, but I don't deny that such plans were submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to move to another topic now. At page 22264, on Wednesday you were talking about in 1999 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, I have to intervene regarding the transcript because the witness said: "I really don't know ..." And we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is an answer: "So I really don't know whether it was or General Lukic who approved those plans." The word missing is "Stevanovic." Is there some other inaccuracy?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But he concluded -- but he concluded his answer with:"I really don't know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's simply a question of twice he said it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1999 you told us about these anti-terrorist activities, and once the order on subordination came out, police units then started receiving not only the maps but also the orders, or the "zapovesti," correct, after late April?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that, and I saw that in the course of preparations, I saw that the order was addressed to the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see that? Did that have a heading coming from the Pristina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we're referring to the time when the war started and when resubordination started.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And did you also see the signature block on those orders?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the best of my recollection, on every document of the Pristina Corps it said commander of the Pristina Corps and there was a signature to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I think the witness said quite clearly on page 36, in line 23, that he saw those documents when he was being proofed, page 36, line 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He never said that it's for the first time. Please, I ask -- kindly ask my colleague to point where this witness said it was for the first time. He did say that he saw them during the preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, this needs to be clarified. Will you deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, you heard that discussion. In addition to seeing these documents during your preparation, did you see them at some earlier point in time, and in particular did you see them in 1999 during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I also saw the orders, but I didn't go into detail. It wasn't I who dealt with that; it was others. But along with the maps I did see the orders as well at the time when there was resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned, regarding the issue of resubordination or subordination, that there were problems you said at I think 22273 that problems arose initially because certain VJ officers believed that anything that belonged to the MUP and that happened to be within their area of responsibility should be resubordinated to the VJ. And on Wednesday, you were asked several questions about this. I understand that you personally can't give us the names of who you referred to when you say "certain VJ officers" who had the misunderstanding, but can you give us the names of some of your MUP people who told you about certain VJ officers who had a misunderstanding? Who told you about this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was General Obrad Stevanovic who told me this, and that's how I know how there came to be different interpretations and disagreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You at page 22275 were asked if you had any information about paramilitary formations in Kosovo or volunteers, and you said as far as you know there weren't any paramilitaries and within the police there weren't any volunteers and that's something that the law does not allow for. But you -- I think you told us you were aware of this incident in -- regarding a killing in Kosovo Polje of some civilians by Skorpions under Slobodan, Boca, Medic. Did you know about that? It happened early during the war, in the late days of March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I heard about such an incident, such an event, but not in Kosovo Polje, it was in Podujevo, so I don't know if we're referring to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I may have misspoken, but your understanding was that that included some Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I heard about the Skorpions only later on when they were tried, when they were put on trial for certain crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So when you first heard about this event in Podujevo, who did you hear had been involved in it? Was it members of the SAJ reserve force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard, that it had been done by members of the reserve force of the SAJ, the S-A-J, and that immediately after that incident they were sent back from Kosovo and Metohija and that later on criminal reports were filed against them and that they were prosecuted, but I can't tell you what happened next and how it all ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever talk about or hear about that from Colonel Zivko Trajkovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Didn't he have responsibility for the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zivko Trajkovic was the commander of the SAJ. I don't know if he's still there or if he's retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But he was the commander in 1999 during the war, right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Were you aware that Rade Markovic had reported in mid-May 1999 that some Arkan's were present in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Rade Markovic was a chief of the state security at the time, so I don't know what information he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to move to another topic. There was a discussion about armbands that were used by the MUP at different times. You mentioned the Perovic incident of this poor man from the Pec SUP. When did that happen? When was he kidnapped and killed, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, before the terrorist activities started in 1998, this is what I recall but it's hard to be precise, it's been a long time since then and I'm not able to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. One more meeting I wanted to ask you about is Exhibit P1990, this is 17 February 1999 meeting. I can hand you a hard copy of this one. It's shorter than most. I don't see your name on the list of attendees for the meeting, but it does say all members of the Pristina MUP staff. So does that mean you were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you look at this document before you came to court to testify? Was it shown to you during your preparation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did. Like I said, I looked a large -- I looked at a large number of documents and I cannot remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could look, I think it's -- if we could scroll toward the bottom of page 1 in the B/C/S. General Lukic opened a meeting and is talking about things, and you'll see a reference to the RPO, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After there there's a sentence that says: "The service has increased its activities in towns," and, Your Honours, I'm in the middle of page 2 of the English. "The service has increased its activities in towns. The annual meetings attended by the head of staff and the deputy head of staff were devoted to last year's work and engagement and determined further tasks and activities of the service." The deputy head of staff, that means you, right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were these annual meetings? Are these annual meetings in the towns involving local defence preparations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were working meetings that were held every year at the -- at all secretariats for internal affairs, not just in Kosovo and Metohija, but also in Vojvodina and Serbia proper, where the annual work analysis was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the plan for the forthcoming period as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, there are no plans for the forthcoming period in these annual reports because the plans for next year are done separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, this sentence says that they were devoted to last year's work and engagement and determined further tasks and activities of the service. Doesn't that mean you're talking about what you're going to do in the coming period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about these annual meetings at the secretariats, this is something that I cannot really talk about because the work is planned by the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But it says these meetings were attended by you and Mr. Lukic and they were devoted to last year's working engagement and determine further tasks and activities. You went to these meetings, right, that's what it says?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is something that is set down by the secretariats generally speaking, detailed annual plans of work are made, and the practice is that the headquarters of the ministry for internal affairs from Belgrade sends someone to attend those working meetings of the secretariats for internal affairs throughout the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia, and General Lukic and myself attended those meetings pursuant to instructions from the ministry because we were already in Pristina so that people would not have to be sent separately from Belgrade for those meetings. That is the only reason that we took part in those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could go down to about the third or fourth line from the bottom of the page you see above the number 4.000 policemen, that sentence begins -- my translation says: "The staff plans to carry out three mopping-up operations in the Podujevo, Dragobilje, and Drenica areas and has allotted around 4.000 policemen, around 70 policemen of the OPG, and around 900 police reservists." Do you recall what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, and I think I talked about that over the previous days, this was an action that was planned by the Pristina Corps to be carried out at those three locations, and in view of this number of members that is stated here, this is probably something that was given by Lieutenant Dusko Jovanovic to the corps so that they could plan. But I don't recall if the action was actually carried out. I don't think that it was, but I cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you may have to go on to the next page of the B/C/S, but the next sentence says: "On Saturday, 20 February 1999 a meeting of the staff will be held with all police unit detachment commanders for further consultations about their engagement." Reading those two things together, Colonel, this seems to me this is an example of the MUP staff carrying out one of its tasks under that decision of 16 June 1998 to organize and manage the engagement of organizational units in complicated security actions or otherwise. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You disagree; let me move on to something else. I want to try and finish before the break, if I can. Okay. Let me just do this to finish up. We talked about the Joint Command a couple of times before, and we showed you that page from the notes of meetings of the Joint Command and you went to a meeting on the 22nd of October, 1998. My question was: How did you come to attend that meeting? Who told you -- well, did somebody tell you to go to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently, General Lukic was not at that meeting because then I wouldn't have been there. I was probably invited at the meeting by somebody, I cannot remember who it was, but Stevanovic was probably there so he said, Let's go to the meeting. This is probably the reason why I attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the minutes -- the meeting notes reflect maybe ten other occasions where General Lukic was not present, but as best you recall this is the only one time, the single time, that you attended, right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from what I recall, it was just that one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And let me ask you with some trepidation two more questions that may require me to refer to P978. Were you aware, did you receive any bulletins or reports from the so-called Joint Command regarding the security situation in October or November 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you Exhibit P1197, and there is a second one, Your Honours, in P1203 but to save time I'm going to try and just use this first one. Colonel, I'll hand you a hard copy. I think if you'll go to the second page of the document you have there -- yeah. You see in the upper left it says Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. It has a strictly confidential number 1142-134 dated 20 November 1998. It's entitled operations report, and it has intelligence and security situation, and then I will tell you it goes on and talks about activities of the terrorist forces against the army, against the MUP, against the population, and it also talks about the engagement of units of the army and the MUP in some detail. Did you ever see this document or any of these kind of operations reports in either 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will refer to Exhibit P948 at page 147.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Phil Coo near the bottom of the page asked: "Do you know if they were putting out Joint Command daily reports?" And on the next page General Lukic's answer: "There was, as I said yesterday, a daily newsletter or bulletin of the Joint Command which was compiled by the Pristina Corps based on features submitted by the state security department, the public security department, military security, that was more or less the content of this daily newsletter, bulletin." Mr. Coo asked: "Was there a distribution on that? Who did it go to?" Mr. -- General Lukic's answer: "Apart from all these users, the same people who also provided the features for the bulletin, which would include the public security department." Does that refresh your memory, did you not see such a bulletin in the MUP staff in late 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing this bulletin, but the fact is that it contains all the data that you mentioned is true, but I don't know who the reports were sent to, also who drafted them. I assume it was the Pristina Corps, but I don't know who the bulletins were done for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we take the break now? I may have no more questions, but if I can review during the break I'll limit myself to five minutes or so after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Mijatovic, you may have answered this already, but from July 1998 until June 1999, how often were you away from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I remember, it was generally once a month for a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is addressed to Mr. Hannis and particularly Mr. Lukic, but as you know the Appeals Chamber has made a decision about the impact of things said in statements by one accused in relation to the case against other accused, and therefore the point applies to everyone. We're inclined to think that this document P948 requires to be translated by CLSS, if that can be arranged. Now, it's not the longest of interviews, as was pointed out, but it would also be helpful if we didn't translate the bits that don't matter. Is there room for parties identifying parts of this that they're entirely satisfied with in its present state because they're really of no particular significance in the trial and identifying the bits that really need to be reviewed and translated again; or is that just out of the question and something we shouldn't even contemplate?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, one part that comes immediately to mind is the beginning of the interview and every time after there's a break in the recording Mr. Curtis goes through the litany of advising Mr. Lukic of his rights, et cetera, sometimes that takes two pages each time. So if the Defence are satisfied with that, I don't think that needs to be translated again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you would consider this over the weekend and on Monday -- well, let's say Tuesday let us know the extent to which it is clear that we need to have this retranslated, and try to avoid unnecessary work. Mr. Fila, if it can be done that way, by positively identifying the bits that need to be rather than negatively excluding the bits that are okay, fine, that would be better. Mr. Mijatovic, we have to break again for half an hour. Would you leave the courtroom with the usher. We'll resume at 20 past 11.00.
