utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, indeed, but I take it you have no other comment to make on that, Mr. Aleksic, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a comment, of course I do. First of all, Mr. Fila used the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly, in your decision dated the 28 of November that my colleague Mr. Sepenuk mentioned, you did say indeed on page 3, or rather, page 4 of this decision that this document was not offered through the witness or are there any indications in our motion that it will be introduced through the witness and, generally speaking, concerning the knowledge and what is stated in this news article. During the examination yesterday -- no, the day before yesterday, Mr. Fila on page 44 of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that I can understand this, what is your position on it and then we'll hear your submissions in support of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am opposed to the objection, and I think that I have a basis for this not being admitted. Mr. Sepenuk is against having this admitted, if I understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Sepenuk is simply pointing out that it's now admitted, but it's admitted simply as an indicator of knowledge or notice being given and that it will not be used, he contends, to establish the truth of the statements in the article. Now, do you take a different view?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to add in relation to that, the witness was asked today on page 69, lines 11 through 17, whether he knew what persons these were and who they belonged to. Mr. Lukic said, were they only from the army or from the police and he said, Yes, yes, I know these people who committed crimes were from different structures, the army, the police, and some third quarters. So he did not confine himself only to not knowing anything about this. That was my point. And then I'm opposed to what my colleague Mr. Sepenuk said, but I wanted to add this that the witness did have something to say in relation to the content of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I follow that, but that really doesn't take the matter any further. What is your objection to Mr. Sepenuk's position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the objection. I misunderstood Mr. Sepenuk, if that is -- well, it was my understanding that he was against having this document admitted into evidence. I misunderstood Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What the witness was saying in the quotation that you've given us is that from his personal knowledge crimes were being committed by people from different structures, and that's his evidence and the newspaper article takes that matter no further as far as we are concerned as a matter of fact. Now, Mr. Fila, do you have anything to say on this or are you content with Mr. Sepenuk's position?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I am content, but I don't understand what this is all about. This accompanying document was written by this gentleman and that's the only thing I asked about, and I really don't understand why all this confusion, I don't understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, that completes your marathon. Thank you for coming to give evidence here. You may now leave the court with the usher and you do not require to return.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I wish you success in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, our next witness is Mr. Milos Deretic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Ivetic on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Deretic. For purposes of the record I would first ask you to introduce yourself to the members of the panel.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. My name is Milos Deretic. I was born on the 18th of July, 1954, in Podujevo. From 1955 onwards, I was living in Pristina, where I completed my elementary school, high school, and the electro-technical faculty. And after graduation I became an electronics and telecommunications engineer. In Kosovo, or rather, in Pristina, I was living until the second half of June when for well-known reasons I had to leave the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and relocated with my family to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already given us an overview of your educational background. Could you also briefly highlight for us your employment within the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, including some of the positions that you held during the course of that employment.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of February, 1982, I began working in the then-provincial SUP in the communications department of the provincial SUP, and I was a systems engineer. In 1993 I was appointed chief of the communications sector of the Pristina SUP, and I remained at that post until June 1999. My other duties, once I moved to Belgrade, were at the administration for communication of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, where in 2001 I was appointed as chief of the communications administration at the seat of the ministry. I remained at that post until the 31st of December, 2006, when I was able to retire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. For the purposes of the next few questions I would ask you to focus on the time-period of the years 1998 to the -- to 1999, and specifically with respect to 1998 through the 31st of May, 1999. What was your specific position and function within the Serbian MUP during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: As I said, in 1998/1999 I was chief of the communications section of the Pristina SUP, and then from the time I was appointed as chief of the section we provided logistical and technical support in communications to the MUP staff in Pristina. All of this -- well, briefly from the 1st of June, 1999, I was a member of the MUP staff along the communications line. Of course, if I may add, this task in the communications section of the SUP Pristina was pursuant to the instructions of the MUP communications service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. For purposes of the transcript, Your Honours, at page 97, lines 11 and 12, I believe the witness said he provided support along the communication line of service to the MUP staff. Perhaps that could be clarified by re-listening to the tape and having CLSS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think you could clarify it now by asking a little more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because obviously this is important what he was doing in relation to the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me -- let me ask the question this way, sir. Within your function in 1998 and 1999 within the Pristina SUP, to which organizational unit or structure of the RJB did you report to and who managed your work?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: According to the rules of internal organization of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, at the seat of each secretariat, or rather, secretariats were formed as territorial organizations of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. Each secretariat at its seat had an organizational unit of -- for communications. The Pristina SUP had a communication section of the SUP, and I belonged to the secretariat of internal affairs in Pristina. In view of this vertical-horizontal principle of organization and the way assignments in the ministry were carried out, I, in order to realize daily work assignments, was responsible to the chief of the Pristina SUP and of course along the line of work also to the authorised administration at the seat of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you first dealt with this matter, you're translated into English on two occasions as referring to the MUP staff. Now, what were your comments about your relationship with the MUP staff in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 1993, when I was appointed as chief of the department for the Pristina SUP communications, among other things, that communications section, the staff of the section, were duty-bound to provide this logistical support, amongst other things, also to the staff because if we look at the rule on internal organization of the MUP the SUP Pristina communications department, according to that rule of internal organizations, also carries out assignments from the sphere of communications for the needs of other secretariats in the area of Kosovo and Metohija so that it was quite logical and normal to have the duty that the communications department, since it was responsible for the functioning of the system of communications in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, for the main communications systems to according to the instructions of the administration for communications to take over this eventually stuff for the needs of the staff or the communications sections to carry out some of these things if required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will help us greatly if you can be as brief as possible in your answers. You also said that from the 1st of June, 1999, you were actually a member of the MUP staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 1st of June, 19 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And for the information of the Court and for the record, what the witness talked about the SUP Pristina having responsibility for communications issues relating across the whole of the secretariats of Kosovo and Metohija, that is contained in Article 45 of the rule book that he specified, which is 6D1305 that we will be tendering into evidence. I don't believe it has yet a full translation of the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But that will be submitted by us at some point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deretic, you mentioned a few times here various sections within the SUP and at the ministry seat and lines of work. Could you explain for us a little bit more the various organizational sections or lines of work that existed within the Serbian MUP in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours, but I will have to explain this in a longer story because according to the rule of internal organization of the ministry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is this witness dealing with it? Is there some sort of diagram that can display it or are we going to need him, being a communications man, to deal with all the organizational sections of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're going to explain the functioning of the SUP of Pristina that he was a part of for over -- almost a decade and discussing how the MUP functions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're at the beginning of our case showing how the various structures of the MUP worked and how information and reporting goes up, communications, et cetera, and in particular he started talking about his section; and I think it does need to be stressed because the translation of what he says comes up differently each time. Sometimes he's helping staff, sometimes he's helping the line of work, and sometimes he's helping the section; so I think we need to understand what he means when he refers to sections and lines of work so that it's clear to this Trial Chamber how the MUP functions because all too often we've had witnesses here claiming the MUP is functioning the same as the army, which is not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I may have misunderstood, the question is a general one that he is going to tell us about all organizational sections rather than how communications worked throughout the Serbian MUP. And it is quite difficult to understand why we need to go beyond Kosovo, but if there's a good reason for that, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, I have lost the reference to the page in your answer, but could you please explain for us how the line of work or line of information and line of management relating to the communications sector worked in the SUP Pristina from your department upwards.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I said that as part of the RJB of the Republic of Serbia of MUP there is a communications administration. It manages the work of the organizational units of communication. Its duties include to plan and organize the system of communications for the needs of the entire ministry. As part of these duties, they actually plan the development, organization, and the maintenance of the communications systems, the equipment and the functioning of the communications. They also control and monitor the work within the -- of the communications systems within the secretariats. On the other hand, the section where I was chief, one of the territorial organizations, according to that line of work, was part of the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were there likewise parallel lines of management among the other sections and lines of work that existed within the Pristina SUP which you made reference to earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I don't know. All I can reliably say for the section that I was chief of is that it functioned in such a way in order to carry out its daily assignments I submitted reports and I was responsible to the SUP chief of Pristina. According to the line of work, it was my duty also to inform the communications department at the ministry. I assume that other sections operated in the same way, the other sections that existed in the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How many other sections existed within the Pristina secretariat of interior?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, I can mention the criminal police section, the police section, fire-fighting police section, the section of border police for aliens and administrative affairs. The section for communications, the section for analysis and records and information technology and also the section for common affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, during this time-period of 1998 to 1999, do you have knowledge of whether the Pristina secretariat of interior, whether they had any employees within the police who were non-Serbs, and specifically who were ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, I could mention some names correctly, of employees in my section. I will try. Ahmetaj Skender was the telephone systems engineer in the section; then Ali Hashani, Ilijaz Ahmeti, they were technicians on the telephone system; Abagjik Nexhmedin [phoen] and Selatin Betulahu [phoen] were technicians of the radio systems. Fatmir Kopriva and Hazbija Thaqi [phoen] were operating the telephone exchange; they were telephone exchange operators. That is my section. I could also just say that the communications section of the Pristina SUP numbered about 35 employees. As for the other employees of non-Serb ethnicity at the Pristina SUP, I know that Musuf Sadiki [phoen] was the head of the section in the fire-fighting police department. Ismet Hajziri [phoen] was working in the police section at the ministry seat, he was an inspector, but I don't know exactly which tasks he was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, and you --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Just, I apologise, I see on the transcript that these names of these Albanian colleagues are not correctly written, it's not Musuf but Musa Sadiku, not Sadiki.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Ismet Haziri. It's not Hajziri but Haziri --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Court reporter's after your testimony, sir. What I wanted to ask you is -- strike that. With respect to these ethnic Albanian colleagues that you have named, am I to understand that they remained employed within the SUP throughout the period of the NATO war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: This is hard to say. Individuals did, but some did not. I know that Hazbija Thaqi, a colleague, asked me to be allowed to be relieved of her duties so that she could spend time with her under-aged children. Of course I did that for her and for other colleagues who worked in the communications section because it was quite normal for people to feel afraid for their children, and then we allowed mothers to be evacuated with their children, to be with their families. This is also what I did with my family, I transferred my sons from the Kosmet area also because it was exceptionally risky for them to remain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, getting back for a moment to the role or the duties of the communications section within the Pristina secretariat that you described and which we saw -- which I indicated was pursuant to Article 45 of the rule book on internal organizations. Did this additional function of the Pristina SUP exist even before 1998, that is before the ministerial staff in Pristina under Sreten Lukic was established?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Yes, this obligation of the SUP Pristina communications section existed also in the prior period, and this can be seen in the then-valid rules on internal organization of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. I just want to clarify, it's not just the SUP Pristina communications section that had this duty. The Novi Sad SUP also had the same obligation, the SUP in Nis, the Kraljevo SUP communications sections all had these obligations. Everything was done so that the cost of work and maintenance would be used in the best possible way. The Novi Sad SUP communications section carried out the same jobs for the secretariats in the territory of Vojvodina. The Nis SUP communications section did that for the secretariats in Zajecar, Bor, Pirot, Nis, the one in Kraljevo worked on this for Cacak, Kraljevo SUPs, I think. All of this is actually stated in the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm just waiting for the transcript and the translation to catch up with us. Now, I wanted to ask you with respect to the work of the various sections and departments and the lines of management with respect to the same within the SUP heading upwards towards the MUP in Belgrade, were those establishments altered in any way by the formation of the MUP staff in June of 1998 with Sreten Lukic as the manager or "rukovodilac" of the same?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: As far as the communications section department, no, everything remained just as it was. I cannot say that for sure about the other organizational units, though, but I think that the principle of work stayed in force in the next period, the staff of the MUP could not change something that was defined in the rules. This horizontal and vertical principle was something that had to be respected. The rules were valid at the level of the ministry. It was a basic document that laid down the organization of the ministry and how certain organizational units in the ministry were supposed to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the document actually refer to the MUP staff for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As far as I know, only the possibilities mentioned for the minister of the interior in accordance with the requirements of the service can form a staff, but the staff does not exist as such as an organizational unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, sir, where the ministry staff was located prior to the commencement of the NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: The MUP staff was located in the so-called administrative building of the Pristina SUP. I think it was on the third floor in that building where the other organizational units were located that belonged to the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the MUP staff in Pristina have an independent or stand-alone system of communications?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: This option does not exist. All communications systems of the MUP are built on a single, unified basis for the entire territory of Serbia, and the staff could not get anything else that could have a better function. What existed in Kosovo and Metohija were integral parts of a unified communications system of the ministry. The MUP staff, I know this and I can confirm that, for example, used the SUP Pristina telephone exchange switches, and they used units in the radio network that was used in the Kosovo and Metohija. They used public telephone networks that were operating in Pristina. Dispatches were convoyed via the authorised services of the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to each one of those in time. I would first like to show you, since it came up in questions from the honourable Trial Chamber, Exhibit P1811. And as we wait for this to come up, sir, I think you'll see this to be a decision on the composition of the ministry staff for prevention of terrorism from the 31st of May, 1999, and on page 2 of the Serb and page 1 of the English we see you mentioned and it lists your position. When you testified that you became a member of the MUP staff, is this the date that you became an effective member and the duties that you accepted as a member of the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Senior advisor Milos Deretic, that's me, and this is the decision handed to me I think on the 1st of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this document states that SUP chiefs and CRDB had -- are to be part of the composition of the MUP staff. To your knowledge were any employees of the RDB sector ever actually members of the ministry staff in Pristina in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: In all these assignments, according to the communications line, the department or section for communications and I myself operated; but I really have no knowledge that there were representatives of the RDB in the MUP staff. I simply don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I should probably have remembered this, but who was your predecessor as chief of signals at the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Cankovic in the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to be clear, sir, who were the head or manager of the MUP staff and his deputy in 1998 up until the date of this decision that we have before us?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I know that the manager was Sreten Lukic and his deputy was Miroslav Mijatovic. Until the 1st of June, 1999, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, Judge Kamenova is asking me how is it possible to be asking a question like this at this stage? This trial is never going to end. That seems to you to have to be asked yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the Office of the Prosecution confronts witness after witness with documents stating that someone else was the deputy head of the MUP staff, so until that question is satisfied and until my client is released from custody a free man, I think I am allowed to ask questions and present -- confront the evidence that the Office of the Prosecution time and time again is presenting before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, we can live without the drama. Who is the other deputy suggested?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: David Gajic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And he's the one actually named in the order; is that right, the order in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In one of the orders in 1998. We're about to go into another order from 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could move to that other order I want to talk about P1252. This was a document that I believe was utilised by the Prosecution and by other Defence counsel in these proceedings dated the 11th of May, 1998, and I would direct your attention to the second page in the Serb original and the English translation as well. And once we see this, sir, we'll see I think your name as the assistant manager for communications. And the question I have for you is very simple: Did you, in fact, ever receive such a decision and were you tasked as a member of the ministry staff in 1998, as this Prosecution document would suggest?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: No. I saw this document for the first time when it was shown to me during my proofing session before this testimony. I assert with full responsibility that I never saw it before and that such a document was never handed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we see the name on this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's the second page in Serbian and in English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can we go over the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In item number 10, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the document look genuine to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I'm really no expert for the analysis and assessment of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you've never seen a document like this before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have seen documents of the ministry, they have a seal and a stamp and a signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you seen Djordjevic's signature before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, could we move now to your speciality and technical issues relating to that speciality. What types of communications systems existed within and were used within the Serbian Ministry of the Interior in 1998 and 1999 in Pristina and in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: These systems can be divided in two main groups: Telephone systems and radio systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. If we could first focus on the telephony systems. Can you tell us, please, what specific telephone systems were within use within the MUP of Serbia, including the organizational and other units in 1998 and 1999 in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: The MUP of the Republic of Serbia is building a telephone network for this special purpose on the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia, and this telephone system is organized in such a way that it consists of telephone switchboards located in the headquarters of the secretariats and they are owned by the MUP of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for what type of communications was this telephone system utilised and how did it differ from ordinary civilian use telephone systems?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: This telephone system was used to transmit speech messages, oral messages, which have a slightly higher degree of priority or confidentiality. Quite simply because this system was felt to be more reliable than the public system only because it was under the constant supervision of expert teams of the ministry and appropriate protection measures were taken. To put it more clearly, it's an ordinary telephone network, in fact, of the same sort that is used by public telephone companies, such as telecom or city authorities. The only difference is that the switchboards are located in secretariat buildings, in secretariat facilities. They are popularly referred to as a special telephone network. Policemen like using these expressions, but, in fact, it's just an ordinary telephone connection, as in any other telephone network. They call each radio station a Motorola, for example, even though it's not, there are differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Were there any other organizations using the same telephonic network, apart from the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Telephone connections or hook-ups from this ministry telephone network were used, for example, by representatives of the government in Belgrade, presidents of municipalities or mayors, representatives of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you pleased explain for us the method by which written messages or telegrams or dispatches would be sent within the MUP of Serbia on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I have to start once more from this singleness of the MUP communications system. On the territory of Kosovo-Metohija, the MUP did not have its own separate system, these were all parts of a single system built to cover the entire territory of Serbia. So to transmit written messages the so-called telegraph system was organized. The configuration of that network resembles very closely the configuration of the telephone network. The difference is that the telegraph switchboards are used which use special codes or encryptions to transmit written messages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If a member of the public telephoned the SUP in Pristina, was there some complicated arrangement to get through or was the system linked automatically to the public telephone system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Incoming calls from the town, for example, when a party is calling the ministry, it first comes to the mediator -- the exchange; that is, a citizen could not get through to a representative of the ministry directly. They would first have to come -- call the exchange and then at the exchange switchboard the telephone operator would ask who they wanted to speak to and they would say, I want Milos Deretic or I want extension such and such and then the operator would put them through. So members of the public could not call up a member of the ministry directly, on a direct line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not unusual in any system. What if you wanted to telephone your wife to say you're coming home for your dinner, do you just lift the phone and you can phone directly out to your own home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we spoke about incoming calls to the Pristina SUP. Outgoing calls, when I was calling from the SUP, would work differently. I would dial 0 and then I would dial my number. So I would not have to go through the operator. I could call directly, whereas incoming calls would take place the way I've described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That all sounds like what happens in any other telephone system, but -- anyway, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You'll see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, your own telephone will be special numbers, will it not be at your house, numbers linked with the exchange directly even though you dial 0, but these will be special numbers, not the public numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to clarify. We were speaking about the special-purpose telephone network. It's a network of the closed type. You do not use it to communicate with the public. To communicate with the public, there is an in-house switchboard, a PRBX local switchboard for both incoming and outgoing phone calls where members of the SUP or the ministry could communicate with the public. So these would be two quite separate switchboards. One would be local and not connected to the secretariat network, whereas the other one was connected to the special-purpose MUP network.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I hope you can clarify it all if it's important. It will become clear once we get to the period of the war what all this means.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right now I would like to focus on the other aspect that you mentioned, the mobile or radio systems of communication, and I would ask you to explain for us what mobile or radio systems of communication existed within the MUP of the Republic of Serbia in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: First I have to say that these radio networks and radio systems are organized in compliance with the territorial organization of the ministry and in accordance with the domain of work of the ministry. The frequencies used to organize these radio networks are used based on the plan for the purpose and distribution of frequencies, which is proposed in every state by the appropriate ministry, in Serbia it's the ministry for telecommunications, and it's adopted by the government. Frequency resources are defined for every user of the radio system in a state. This plan also includes separate frequency ranges for the needs of the army, of the MUP -- or the MUP which we used to organize such radio networks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was the use of these radio frequencies and systems further regulated within the MUP internally?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Yes. The manner of use of radio communications in the ministry is defined in the instructions on the use of radio and telephone communications systems. I think it was published in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, continue.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that an integral part of these instructions is the directory of users of the telecommunications system and radio system where the signals are listed, the numerical structure of these signals, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you please take a moment to explain for us the use of call-signs in radio communications of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia from the time-period 1998 to 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: For radio communications to function normally, it's quite normal for every participant in radio communications when establishing a connection to introduce himself with his call-sign. Every organizational unit of the ministry had its general call-sign. On the territory of Kosovo, for example, the Pristina SUP had Sitnica as its call-sign. The SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica was Ibar; the SUP of Pec was Bistrica; the SUP of Djakovica was Drim; the SUP of Urosevac was Sara; the SUP of Gnjilane was Cer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can ask you to please then tell us also about the use of code words in the course of radio communications, and in regard to that please advise us whether these radio communications were, in fact, secure.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, one should know that the radio systems that the MUP of the Republic of Serbia organized on its entire territory, including Kosovo and Metohija, were analog in technology. Such equipment and such radio communications can be listened in to or jammed very easily. For an information -- a piece of information which is confidential to be transmitted by a radio communication without it being made available to undesired listeners, the police often used encrypted or coded messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And without belabouring the point, can you tell us some examples of such code words. For instance, we've had reference to Sivo.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Usually -- yes, I remember detachments of the PJP units usually used a combination of colours and numbers to transmit a message without it being available to everyone. For example, there was grey zero, which meant there are injured; grey five meant there are dead; red two meant we are expecting an attack. These were the codes used from the code books. Green also meant something, and then green with a number following would describe a situation in which the unit currently found itself, whether they were under fire or had a damaged vehicle or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was there any law governing the misuse of radio frequencies? Was that codified in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, every state regulates its frequency resources in its penal code. I'm no lawyer, but I think that in the penal code of the Republic of Serbia there are legal sanctions against anyone who owns or uses a radio station without authorisation. And abuses of the system, or rather, problems arising between users of various radio systems are dealt with by the ministry. So my answer is yes, penal code.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have knowledge of any illegal transmissions or misuse of radio frequencies in 1999 whereby messages were sent in Albanian for Albanians to leave Kosovo and Metohija and the measures taken by the Serb authorities in response to this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that representatives of the ministry of telecommunications used to come and see me in Pristina asking me to help them implement their assignment, which was to locate the radio station called "free Kosovo," which somewhere from the territory of Metohija broadcast its radio programme. This radio station was conducting an aggressive propaganda campaign, introducing fear among the Albanian population and clearly calling on Albanians to move out of Kosovo and Metohija. My knowledge of this follows from my conversations with the representatives of the ministry of telecommunications. I want to make that clear. I personally did not listen to those broadcasts of that radio station because we couldn't hear it in Pristina. It was broadcast from the territory of Metohija, and the radio station constantly changed its location. It was mounted on a vehicle, so the team from the measurement centre was unable to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge or information as to the source of the propaganda from this Free Kosovo radio station? Was it the work of an officially licenced radio operator or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: Had the radio station had a licence, the members of the telecommunication ministry would not have been hunting after it because they have to deal with these things. The station did not have an operating permit. It was an illegal station, most probably of Albanian separatists of their liberation army of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there documents about this, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I don't have a document at hand about this. We have -- we can ask for the Government of Serbia to send more documents if you like about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a matter for you. Do we have a time-scale as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe I had said 1999 before the NATO strikes, but we can ask the witness to clarify that if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you clarify the time-period when you have personal knowledge of this activity that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: It was probably in the period before the bombing because I know that at the time I was in my office in the Pristina SUP building. After the bombardment I couldn't return there anymore, so it must have been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, would you tell us a little bit about the official -- the specific radio networks of the MUP, that is to say how they were used within the various organizational structures, the various SUPs, on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and what coverage or range these networks had.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: The plan of distribution and use of radio frequencies, the MUP had two ranges for the organization of its radio communications. One was on the VHF and the other was on the UHF waves. I could provide more detail, but I believe that it is not important. The needs of each secretariat called for the formation of a VHF radio network, as a part of which the secretariat seat had communications with its sectors of internal affairs and police stations in their area. So when we were drafting or making these radio networks, we asked for the traffic to be possible at least by fixed stations. Also each secretariat in the area of Kosovo and Metohija had an organized network on the UHF system. This is a system from 450 to 456 megahertz, which is much more favourable for covering urban areas. And in this UHF network you had policemen working who were carrying out their assignments in urban areas, in the town areas. So this UHF communication could not be used for longer distances because it was intended only for the city, for urban areas. So each secretariat in the Kosovo area had its network organized in this particular way. Of course until the bombing, these more powerful radio stations, fixed radio stations, were able to establish radio connections with the services on duty of the secretariat seats, not their outlying branches or belonging organizational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about hand-held radios or I think you had used the term Motorolas, what was their position within this radio system of communications and what was their coverage or range?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I said that in these radio networks, the users of the ministry radio network system could not be guaranteed a secure line with hand-held radios. Each user was told that a fixed stationary station was all right, but a hand-held station was possible to use up to a certain range but not for other ranges, it depended on the range and the frequencies. If I may add, they go along the line of optical vision. So any obstacle of a geographical nature, a hill or anything of that nature, interferes for -- with these radio waves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Allow me to ask a very specific question about these hand-held radio units. Based on the factual and technological circumstances you've described for us, was it possible by means of a hand-held radio for police forces involved in an action outside of Pristina to engage in real-time communication with the MUP staff located in Pristina or for someone in Pristina to follow the radio chatter on these hand-held radios in the course of an action?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about the period before the bombing, then I must first explain that the police units while they were carrying out an action always worked using hand-held radios in the so-called simplex way of operation, meaning direct communication, station to station, locally. These simplex communications were good to use in micro locations, and the range of these connections would be up to 2 kilometres, depending again on the configuration of the terrain. This means that from Pristina such communications could not be monitored. Pristina could perhaps receive information if the detachment commander possibly from some location used a call station to call a radio user in Pristina, with the assumption that at that location it was possible to hear that working channel that was possibly monitored in Pristina. We're talking about the period until the bombing. After the bombing, it was a whole other story.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before we get to the bombardment I'd like to ask you one further question. Did the MUP, either on the territory of Kosovo-Metohija or the rest of Serbia, have any alternative or special planned means of communication, either telephony or radio, to be used or implemented in the event of a state of war, which would -- which disrupted the regular means of communication?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: No. According to its formation, the MUP is not intended for war situations at least I believe that it should perform its work in peacetime conditions, work conditions and for that reason the concept of our system of communication was such that the equipment was intended for stationary conditions of work; and this implied, for example, if we wanted some equipment of the systems communication to begin working, first we had to ensure and technically prepare room to install the equipment and then we needed to provide reliable energy supplies and reserve energy supplies to run this equipment, cables. Also the appropriate antenna installations. So looking at it in that way, the MUP did not have equipment that was intended for wartime action or operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could focus on the time-frame of the NATO bombings. Can you tell us if during that time-period there were instances of blocking or jamming of MUP radio communications by enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: It was a daily occurrence at all radio channels used by the MUP. I said -- I talked about analog technology of our radio systems. Practically anyone who had a radio station for that range could monitor our radio channels and jam them. Of course this was done even by representatives of the international organizations. I'm familiar with a case when an international organization or the international organization of the Red Cross had radio stations with our working channels. Of course there were many colleagues, Albanians, who had left the ranks of the MUP of Serbia and at least those who were technically trained knew the frequencies that the MUP was using for its radio communications. And once you knew that, it's not a problem, it's not a technical problem, to programme the radio station with these radio channels. Also, I know that a lot of radio stations were seized from killed or wounded police members so that the KLA used the stations to eavesdrop and jam our radio communications on a permanent basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the jamming of radio communications. How could that be accomplished? I think you said even that it was not a technical problem. How could that jamming of the Serbian MUP's radio communications be most effectively undertaken?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I don't know how familiar you are with the organization of these radio systems. In analog technology practically one frequency is one working channel. So if we had, as we had, for example, 58 channels or -- used by the Pristina MUP members, it would be enough for one user with bad intentions to place that station on receive mode and hold the receive mode for a while, then that channel would automatically be blocked. Because according to the radio networks, the radio channels, it was possible only to have one radio connection at the time. So you have alternative regime -- evidently I am talking too fast, and I am being warned and this is why I stopped. So the jamming could be done very simply. I hope that you understood me, in what way this could be done. The jamming was possible only -- it was possible by non-professionals as well. Of course if somebody wished to disrupt this intentionally or deliberately, then the possibilities were very wide, then you could block the whole frequency range used by the MUP and then all the connections would be cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we've had evidence here, sir, about the bombing of the SUP building in Pristina, specifically at the beginning of the war on March 29th, 1999. Could you please tell us what the consequences of the NATO strike on the SUP Pristina building were with respect to the telephonic and radio communication capabilities of the SUP or the MUP staff that had been housed in that same building.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: The Pristina SUP facility was where this special telephone exchange was located. In the transmissions system organizations, the switchboards from other secretariats in the area of Kosovo and Metohija were linked to this switchboard or exchange. So if somebody from Djakovica wanted to get in touch with Nis via telephone, first of all, they reached Pristina and that connection was transferred towards the rest of Serbia. In other words, when the building was knocked down, the telephone exchange in the Pristina SUP building was destroyed, which meant that the lines in this special telephone network were disrupted. So the speech communications, the telephone connections from the SUPs in the area of Kosovo and Metohija to Pristina and the other parts of Serbia were disrupted, and then you just had the public telephone connections remaining, while the SUP telephone connections were cut. As for the radio system, the Pristina SUP building had an antenna pole 60 metres high with accompanying antenna systems, and this was also destroyed during the bombing of the SUP building in Pristina, which means that those connections that we could use from Pristina to the duty services of the secretariat in the Kosovo and Metohija area were no longer working.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you describe for us whether there were any radio relay stations located on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija that made up part of the MUP radio communication network and how they were affected by the NATO bombing campaign and how the MUP communications would likewise have a resultant effect?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: After the bombing of the Pristina SUP building and even before that, the transmission location of Goles was bombed. At the time, the system transmission node was damaged that the telecom had at that facility. Telecom, as the public and sole operator of fixed telephones in the state of Serbia had organized systems in the Metohija area, radio relay systems, that were used for public telephone communications. In this way, connections were realized, I'm talking about telecom connections, via the radio relay area in Kosovsko Pomoravlje, I'm talking about Gnjilane. So these Telecom communication nodes were at Goles once that transmission facility was destroyed, it was practically -- we had the places of Pec, Djakovica, Prizren, and Gnjilane with their environs, they were left without public telephone and all other forms of communication. Of course, at the same time the MUP could not have any communication, I'm talking about dispatch communications, the telegraph system, which was also affected by the telecom broadcast or transmissions system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Goles location. Were there other relays and when, if at all, were they attacked by NATO, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC
utterances.text: I can mention some of the key emission locations that the MUP used to locate its radio equipment. Burovacki Breg, that was Grmija near Pristina, Goles, we know where that is. At some 30 kilometres from Pristina, that's where the transmission location was, then the location Stari Trg near Kosovska Mitrovica on the Mokra Gora mountain there was another transmission location, then Bukova Glava on Sar Planina Mountain, then Kursumlijska Banja, Zeleni Vrh near Gnjilane. All of these were key broadcast locations used by the MUP to location its radio equipment via which it organized its radio network.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at the half-hour mark. Would now be a good time to pause? I have approximately 15 minutes or so left of direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we should pause there, Mr. Ivetic. I've had a chance just to review some of the evidence there on the leadership of the MUP staff, and you're quite right it is a significant issue who is the deputy chief of the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But of course not apparently who was the chief of the -- anyway. Mr. Deretic, that brings our proceedings for today to an end. We have to rise now and resume on Monday, that will be at 9.00 on Monday morning in this courtroom. Over the weekend it's a strict rule that you should have no communication with anyone about the evidence in this case, that's any of the evidence, evidence you have given, will give, and evidence that anyone else has given or might give. You can talk about anything else to whoever you like, but no communication about the evidence in this case whatsoever. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you at 9.00 on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.
